slides.say: A number is divisible without remainder by both ten and twenty-five. What is the greatest number that is guaranteed to divide it?

So we don't know the number. All we know is that ten divides it, and twenty-five divides it. And they ask, what's the biggest number we can be sure divides it? [short pause] We'll solve it three ways, with primes, with the smallest number that fits, and with a short formula.
at: biggest number we can be sure

slides.say: [short pause] If ten divides the number, the number contains all of ten. And if twenty-five divides it, it contains all of twenty-five. So let's break both. Ten is two times five, and twenty-five is five times five.

Now, why not just multiply ten by twenty-five? Let's see it on simpler numbers. A number that divides by three and by seven surely divides by twenty-one, because three and seven share nothing. But a number that divides by three and by nine, does it divide by twenty-seven? Not necessarily. Nine itself divides by three and by nine, and it doesn't divide by twenty-seven. Nine already has the three inside it.
at: that divides by three and by nine

slides.say: The same thing happens here. The five in ten may be the very same five that's inside twenty-five. When there's an overlap, we don't count it twice.
So how many of each prime do I need? Twos, only ten has one, so one two. Fives, ten needs one and twenty-five needs two, and two fives cover both. So every prime at its higher power.
at: every prime at its higher power

slides.say: Two times five squared, two times twenty-five, is fifty. So fifty, choice number three is our answer.
at: choice number three is our answer

slides.say: And now careful with two hundred fifty, the trap. That's ten times twenty-five, the five counted twice. Can we promise it? The number might be just fifty, and two hundred fifty doesn't divide fifty. So choice number four is out.
at: The number might be just fifty

slides.say: [pause] Our second method, the smallest number that fits. A number that's guaranteed to divide must divide every number that fits, so it must divide even the smallest one. So let's find the smallest number that both ten and twenty-five divide. Remember the common denominator from fractions, I run through the multiples of the bigger one.
Multiples of twenty-five. Twenty-five, does ten divide it? No. Fifty, does ten divide it? Yes, fifty is five tens. So fifty is the smallest number that fits.

Now the choices. Twenty-five divides fifty, so it's guaranteed, but it's not the greatest. A hundred and two hundred fifty are bigger than fifty, so they can't divide it. Out. And fifty divides itself, so the greatest guaranteed divisor is fifty, choice number three.
And this smallest common multiple has a name you saw with fractions, the LCM, the least common multiple. So the greatest guaranteed divisor is just the LCM.

[pause] Our third method, a short formula. The GCD times the LCM equals the two numbers multiplied. Why? Multiplying ten by twenty-five counts the shared five twice. Dividing by the GCD, the part they share, takes the extra five off.

Ten times twenty-five is two hundred fifty. The GCD of ten and twenty-five is five, the one five they share. Two hundred fifty over five is fifty. Choice number three again. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
